articles.text: A motion was introduced into the Senate, Tuesday to allow G. C. Moody, senator-elect from the so-called state of Dakota, a seat in the Senate chamber, until the division and admission bill should be decided. The motion was held over until yesterday.
articles.summary: A motion to seat Dakota 'senator-elect' G. C. Moody in the U.S. Senate pending the division and admission bill was held over.

articles.text: The yearly report of the Wells-Fargo express Co., on the amount of gold, silver, copper and lead mined west of the Missouri river, shows a grand total for 1885, in the four metals, of $90,181,260. Colorado is first with a total output of over $21,000,000, California is second, Montana is third, Nevada is fourth, Utah is fifth, Dakota is sixth and Washington is fourteenth and last. California is first, Colorado second, Dakota third and Utah last in gold production.
articles.summary: Wells-Fargo report on 1885 western metal output, with Dakota sixth overall and third in gold.

articles.text: It is plain that the eastern breeders' and farm journals are watching the Denver convention of range cattlemen with Argus eyes. More strongly then than before do we repeat that unless level heads rule the convention, it will do more harm than good. Of course these papers are naturally inimical to range interests and will magnify any point against them. This, however, does not lessen their influence and if the convention is not careful, it will give them an opportunity to do lasting injnry to the range industry.
articles.summary: Editorial warning that the Denver range cattlemen's convention must keep level heads under eastern scrutiny.

articles.text: Nothing new has occurred in reference to the organization of the county. In other words, the Bismarck opposition to the organization of Billings county has so delayed matters that we are compelled to virtually throw away nearly enough money to pay the running expenses of the county for a year, unless the law authorizing the tax is declared unconstitutional. We are in receipt of a letter from a legal friend, however, that fully bears out all we have said on the subject. He advises that the taxes be paid promptly, but only to avoid the five per cent. penalty. He advises, however, that one tax-payer should not pay his taxes and that a test case should be the result, in the expenses of which the whole county should contribute. The reason given in the Cow Boy last spring is also used by our correspondent as an unanswerable objection to the constitutionality of the law: A law was already in force and is now unrepealed by which senior counties receive pay for all expenses incurred in the government of unorganized counties. Consequently, Stark county would receive pay twice for the same services. He also advises that the county should conduct the suits and to that end, should compel the opposition to the organization of the county to publicly state the cause of their opposition, so that their trifling reasons can be exposed and that on the organization of the county, the proper officials should conduct the suit. In case the law was declared unconstitutional, the tax-payers' money could be recovered. In case it was not, the money that would by the other law have gone to Stark county, will be paid direct to Billings county. In either event, our money would be returned to us.
articles.summary: Editorial on the stalled organization of Billings county, blaming Bismarck opposition, and a legal friend's advice to bring a test case against the tax paid to Stark county.

articles.text:
There are some things that make us tired. Two of these are: civil service reform as at present practiced and the howl about the silver dollar. To go into a full discussion of the merits and demerits of each woutd require volumes, to judge by the voluminous way in which both points are treated by the daily press. In a word, Civil service reform is a mis-nomer, because except in minor points, there is nothing to reform. For the last twenty-five years our civil service has steadily improved, until now it is beyond the power of human beings to reform or improve it, except perhaps in the minor point of filling vacancies. The record made by the last administration is unequalled since the world began by any public or private corporation. In all tde thousands and hundreds of thousands of ways the government has of receiving and disbursing money the entire loss and total cost is included in three mills on the thousand dollars. And the civil service which performs such a totally unparalleled feat must needs be reformed. Bosh! The whole thing is a catch-penny device of politicians both Democratic and Republican, to catch votes.

The cry against the silver dollar because it is only worth in silver 79½ cents is equally as "stale, flat and unprofitable." What does any one care what it is worth, so long as it will buy a dollars worth of goods? Wall street does, because Wall street's nest would be nicely feathered if a change were made. And Wall street and its minions in Congress are doing all the howling. Senator Leland Stanford recently gave an unanswerable reply to a senator who was arguing to him that the present silver dollar was worth only 79½ cents: "You say this dollar is worth only 79½ cents. I will give you 99½ cents for 100,000 of them and you can make $20,000 by the operation." At last accounts the trade had not been consummated. It is the sheerest nonsense to meddle with something that is giving perfect satisfaction to the public at large and politicians will burn their fingers fooling with the "dollar of our daddies."
articles.summary: Editorial calling civil service reform a vote-catching device and defending the silver dollar against Wall street.

articles.headline: A Riddle For Stockmen.
articles.text:
My first is first prattled by infantile tongue,
And has often been honored in story and song,
And when men are anxious in search of a wife,
They make friends with my first, to be first in the strife.

My second is two letters with only one sound,
On the clock-face, a figure, it often is found.
May your pocket-book never hold anything less,
And you never will lack a good dinner, I guess.

My last is a large stack of hay I am told,
Tho' the word is not used much, because it's so old.
Yet the man who can't find it with hints in a heap,
Should quit herding cattle and go and keep sheep.

My whole as to gender, is common, I trow,
Tho' 'tis masculine sometimes and feminine now;
It does not belong to a stockman by law,
Yet stockmen all claim it wherever they go.
—[Glendive Independent.
articles.summary: Clipped verse riddle for stockmen from the Glendive Independent.

articles.text: The receipts for last week at the Chicago stock yards included 46,918 cattle, a gain of about six thousand over the previous week. As a consequence, and because also there were no really prime cattle on the market, the price dropped on all classes. The highest price paid was $5.30 for some 1,450 ℔ steers.
articles.summary: Chicago receipts of 46,918 cattle last week; prices dropped on all classes.

articles.text: There is a growing sentiment among cattlemen that the Chicago market was, at least during the last season, under the control of the great packing-house proprietors. With no actual cause whatever, and in the face of diminished receipts, the price would go down in the most mysterious and remarkable way. The heavy buyers may not have pooled and had one or two do all the buying, but they are not at all like men who wouldn't do such things.
articles.summary: Cattlemen suspect the big Chicago packers controlled last season's market.

articles.headline: Barbed Wire Cuts.
articles.text: It may not be generally known that there is a very simple and inexpensive remedy for cuts and bruises on horses and cattle at the command of almost everyone. Furthermore, the remedy is to be relied upon. In cases of fresh cuts or injuries from barbed wire, however severe, or running sores, apply to the wound lime, fresh slacked, of the consistency of thick cream, with a common paint brush. Cover the wound as thick as possible and repeat daily or oftener, if necessary. In a short time, new flesh will form and the wound will heal with hardly a scar. This remedy may seem too simple to do much, if any good. Others may think the lime, applied to a flesh wound, too harsh treatment. One trial, we are confident, will convince the most skeptical.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Clipped Texas Stockman remedy of slaked lime for barbed-wire cuts on stock.

articles.headline: Cure for Blackleg.
articles.text:
We do not know of a solitary instance of the above disease in the Bad Lands, nor is it at all liable to appear among range cattle. It generally attacks only calves and then only when they are in first-class condition, from being kept up and fed. Hitherto, the disease has been considered incurable, but the following treatment, published in the Kansas City Live Stock Indicator is claimed to be an infallible cure. It would be well to preserve it.

"I would take a knife and strike a hole through the dew-lap at the point of the brisket; take a strip of muslin, put some lard on it with as much black hellebore root as would make a pill about the size of a small pea. Fold the muslin so as to put it through like any other seton and tie the ends. It will make a sore that will act as a vaccination. Those who try this will never have any more black-leg."
articles.summary: No blackleg known in the Bad Lands; reprints a Kansas City Live Stock Indicator cure.

articles.headline: To Ride a Broncho.
articles.text:
Great care should be taken in selecting the broncho, the younger and gentler he is, the better. After you have made your selection, throw and tie him; Then bandage his hoofs in a heavy swathing of gunny sacks, for he may accidentally kick you, and when he is up and bucking, your liver is more apt to stay in its place. Then put on the saddle and bridle and blind; then let him up. Now draw the reins over the horn, hobble your stirrups, and put on a pair of buck-straps and a large, soft "roll."

If you have previously padded the seat of your pants and sewed two porous plasters together back to back, place the plasters in the seat of the saddle and yourself on top of them. If you have not made the last two preparations, do so before you attempt to ride.

Now, if you have followed the directions and are in the saddle, take a firm hold of each buck-strap and have the person holding the broncho pull the blinds from his eyes and turn him loose. It is presumed that you have previously taken a few fingers of sand-producer so all you have to do now is to keep cool—and your seat.—[Glendive Independent.
articles.summary: Humorous clipped instructions for riding a broncho, from the Glendive Independent.

articles.summary: Warning that a haystack is not public property.

articles.text: Quite a number of range cattle are making a winter resort of Medora. It would be a good plan for their owners to drive them back where they wouldn't have to rustle so hard for feed.
articles.summary: Range cattle wintering in Medora; owners urged to drive them back.

articles.text: The Luffsey estate has been settled, though how much there was or who received it, was not stated. The only claims are the burial expenses and Frank O'Donald's claim as partner.
articles.summary: The Luffsey estate has been settled.

articles.text: Although the thermometer is not lower than twenty degrees below, to-day is the hardest day on stock that we have had this winter. A keen wind is blowing that on the prairie, must be the worst if it is not the only blizzard of the season.
articles.summary: Thursday is the hardest day on stock this winter, with a keen wind at twenty below.

articles.text: Jack Tisdale, the N. P. track rider reports that the cattle are giving but little trouble between here and Glendive, except at Mingusville. A large herd has gone in there and no effort to drive them out had been successful up to the time when he left.
articles.summary: N. P. track rider Jack Tisdale reports a herd stuck at Mingusville.

articles.text: The present cold snap has in several instances, made the most beautiful frost work it has ever been our lot to see. The frost figures on the window resemble the finest kind of embossed velvet work, raised at least a sixteenth of an inch.
articles.summary: The cold snap has made remarkable frost work on windows.

articles.text: The last ten days has furnished the only hard spell of weather we have had this winter. Rarely has the thermometer been above zero and double figures below has been the rule. Range cattle have drifted considerably, but with the exception of the herd south of Dickinson this drifting has carried them to better feed in more sheltered places.
articles.summary: Ten days of hard cold; range cattle drifting.

articles.text: Geo. Roderick came in from Jamestown Saturday night, but had scarcely arrived when he received a telegram to return immediately. Some time ago we mentioned that Mr. and Mrs. Roderick had started for the latter's home. On the way, she was taken suddenly ill and they were compelled to stop at Jamestown. Here she seemed to be recovering and George ventured on the trip to Medora, where he received the telegram that his wife was much worse. We join heartily with the many Medora friends of Mrs. Roderick in wishing her speedy recovery to the same good health she enjoyed in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Geo. Roderick recalled to Jamestown where his wife is seriously ill.

articles.text: The ice was all put up by Saturday night, making the total amount in the Co's houses here, about 10,000 tons. It is hard to conceive how it could have been put up more economically, except in the one fact of having the ice-houses nearer the dam. The cost, stored in the houses, was a little less than thirty cents per ton. In view of this, the statement of Hough & Dustin of Miles City, that they have been putting up ice at ten cents a ton and would still further reduce the cost to five cents, sounds slightly mythical.
articles.summary: Ice harvest finished: about 10,000 tons in the company's houses at under 30 cents a ton.

articles.text: A letter from a friend in Dickinson states that about fifteen hundred cattle have drifted down below Dickinson and are in bad shape there. The ground over which they are travelling was nearly or quite burned off during last fall and the cattle may be said to be without feed. The recent severe weather would make severe losses in this herd if the range is in as bad condition as our correspondent claims. No brands were mentioned and we have no means of knowing to whom the herd belonged. In all probability it is a mixed herd, representing a number of brands. In any event, a party should be made up immediately to look after them. A total lack of feed, on the exposed prairie, would soon so weaken them that they could not be driven to feed.
articles.summary: About 1,500 drifted cattle without feed below Dickinson.

events.excerpt: Bob Roberts and James Hannigan dissolved partnership, Tuesday.

events.title: C. F. Ellison contracts to put up ice for Roberts and Kennedy
events.summary: C. F. Ellison contracted to put up ice for Bob Roberts and Gill Kennedy.
events.excerpt: C. F. Ellison has contracted to put up ice for Bob Roberts and Gill Kennedy.

events.title: Fred Willard goes to Jamestown to inspect horses
events.summary: Fred Willard went to Jamestown to inspect a lot of horses being taken east.
events.excerpt: Fred Willard went to Jamestown Monday to inspect a lot of horses that were being taken east.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Teacher Simmers introduces competitive class ranking
events.summary: The Medora teacher, Simmers, was arousing good scholarship with a competitive system of rank in classes.
events.excerpt: Much good scholarship is being aroused by teacher Simmers, in a competitive system of rank in classes.

events.title: Train No. 2 kills ten cows near South Heart
events.summary: Five cows were killed outright near South Heart by train No. 2 and five more were so badly hurt they had to be killed.
events.excerpt: Five cows were instantly killed near South Heart last Friday by No. 2

events.title: J. A. VanEeghen and 'Tap' Bemis go to Miles City
events.summary: J. A. VanEeghen and "Tap" Bemis went to Miles City; Bemis has returned while VanEeghen remained.
events.excerpt: J. A. VanEeghen and "Tap" Bemis went to Miles last week.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Refrigerator Car Co. cuts force further for winter
events.summary: The Refrigerator Car Co. further reduced its working force and turned out six or eight teams for the winter.
events.excerpt: The Ref. Car Co. have still further reduced their working force

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Frank Foster contracts to car 500 tons of ice for the railroad
events.summary: Frank Foster contracted with the railroad company to load 500 tons of ice at Medora, probably for Dickinson.
events.excerpt: Frank Foster has made a contract with the railroad company to car for them here, five hundred tons of ice.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Range cattle wintering in Medora town
events.summary: Quite a number of range cattle were wintering in Medora and the paper urged their owners to drive them back where feed was easier.
events.excerpt: Quite a number of range cattle are making a winter resort of Medora.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Luffsey estate settled
events.summary: The Luffsey estate was settled; the only claims were burial expenses and Frank O'Donald's claim as partner.
events.excerpt: The Luffsey estate has been settled, though how much there was or who received it, was not stated.

events.title: Hardest day on stock this winter
events.summary: With the thermometer at twenty below and a keen wind blowing, the paper called the day the hardest on stock that winter, likely the worst blizzard of the season on the prairie.
events.excerpt: to-day is the hardest day on stock that we have had this winter.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: Cattle herd lodged at Mingusville on the N. P. line
events.summary: N. P. track rider Jack Tisdale reported cattle gave little trouble between Medora and Glendive except at Mingusville, where a large herd could not be driven out.
events.excerpt: A large herd has gone in there and no effort to drive them out had been successful

events.date_basis: "the last ten days" before Thu 21 Jan 1886
events.title: Ten-day cold spell; range cattle drift
events.summary: The last ten days brought the winter's only hard spell, rarely above zero and often double figures below; range cattle drifted, mostly to better sheltered feed.
events.excerpt: Rarely has the thermometer been above zero and double figures below has been the rule.

events.title: Geo. Roderick called back to Jamestown by wife's illness
events.summary: George Roderick came in from Jamestown but was telegraphed to return at once because Mrs. Roderick, taken ill on the way to her home, had grown much worse.
events.excerpt: Geo. Roderick came in from Jamestown Saturday night, but had scarcely arrived when he received a telegram to return immediately.

events.title: Medora ice harvest completed: about 10,000 tons
events.summary: The ice was all put up by Saturday night, about 10,000 tons in the company's ice-houses at Medora, at a cost of a little under thirty cents a ton.
events.excerpt: The ice was all put up by Saturday night, making the total amount in the Co's houses here, about 10,000 tons.

events.date_basis: undated item in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; week before issue
events.title: 1,500 drifted cattle without feed below Dickinson
events.summary: A Dickinson correspondent reported about 1,500 cattle drifted below Dickinson onto range burned off last fall; the paper urged a party be made up to look after them.
events.excerpt: about fifteen hundred cattle have drifted down below Dickinson and are in bad shape there.

events.title: Packard and O'Hara dissolve coal-mining partnership
events.summary: A. T. Packard and Patrick O'Hara dissolved their coal-mining partnership by mutual consent; Packard and a new partner continue the business.
events.excerpt: the partnership heretofore existing between A. T. Packard and Patrick O'Hara in the coal-mining business, was dissolved by mutual consent.

events.date_basis: advertisement in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue; opening date not given
events.title: Willard & Keeler open meat market in former Chas. Cook building
events.summary: Willard & Keeler advertised that they had opened a first-class meat market in the building formerly occupied by Chas. Cook, paying cash for game.
events.excerpt: We have opened a first-class meat market in the building formerly occupied by Chas. Cook

events.date_basis: standing advertisement in Thu 21 Jan 1886 issue
events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand advertised: Theodore Roosevelt, proprietor
events.summary: The standing brand advertisement for the Chimney Butte Ranch named Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor and Ferris & Merrifield as managers, with the Maltese cross brand, range six miles south of the N. P. R. R. on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Chimney Butte Ranch. Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor. Ferris & Merrifield, Managers.
